boundary: the release itself: every spatial or temporal memory defect live in the ported 5.36.3, whatever allocator holds the memory
title: Eleven spatial and temporal defects live in Perl 5.36.3, each measured live at the pin and clean at master, with what each arm sees
live_in_pin_note: Liveness is measured in both directions for every case, not inferred: each trigger reports under ASan on a build of the pin's own tree and is silent on the same trigger, same harness and same ASan options on master. The dates alone would not settle it -- four of the eleven fixes are DATED BEFORE the v5.36.3 tag (2023-11-28) and are still absent from it, because they landed on blead and were never backported to the 5.36 maintenance branch. Each case therefore records the ancestry that was actually checked with git merge-base --is-ancestor, in both directions.
note: The population was every commit from v5.36.3 to the master tip that touches both C source and a test (457 of 9537), filtered to the ones whose diff has the shape of a spatial or temporal memory defect and triaged by hand against the pin's sources. All eleven cases here are in scope by construction: this corpus admits only spatial and temporal memory defects, which is the study's scope, so unlike the mruby corpus it carries no null dereferences, type confusions or stack-exhaustion rows. One of the eleven is outside every arm's denominator and says so in its own file: 9e298ab597's trigger passes its own assertion on all four Capstone arms and on CheriBSD with revocation off and on, so the stale slot it needs never exists there; host ASan reports SEGV, so the defect is real but the trigger does not travel. The honest denominator is 10. 254b30e378 carried harness_limit until 2026-10-06 and that is WITHDRAWN: the defect did not execute in a domain because perl-cross installs almost none of the target library (636 pure-Perl modules absent, XSLoader.pm among them), so PerlIO_find_layer("scalar") could not require PerlIO::scalar and the open silently took the generic perlio layer. With the library staged by build-perl-domain.sh the case is caught. sysalloc-bounds is the baseline: per-object heap bounds are what applications get by default since PR #170, so a catch is a case the bounds arm does not fault on. The nested-allocator arm is sublet-svheads, and it protects ONE of Perl's nested allocators -- the SV head arena. The SV bodies, hash entries and OP slabs keep their upstream allocators, so a case whose stale pointer lives in those is out of that arm's reach by construction and its arm entry says so. All five arms are measured. The two revoking arms add DIFFERENT cases and no single Capstone image here has both, because build.py forbids it: --nested with --heap sublet is a ValueError, a nested-allocator arm taking level0 for its separate outer heap. sysalloc-sublet adds 254b30e378, whose stale SvPVX buffer is system-allocator memory; sublet-svheads adds 17535c984a, whose SV head never returns to malloc. Their union is 8, and an image combining them is the obvious next build. cheribsd-revocation reports on 7: it catches 254b30e378 and is blind to 17535c984a for the same reason ASan is, which is this corpus's central result measured a second way. Revocation there is selected per process because the system-wide default kills the guest's own sshd, and every case ran under both settings so the pair controls the knob.
